opening_message: There's a small tree in my yard that looks kind of scraggly. Does anyone know what this actually is?

slots.name: fruit_description
slots.value: It gets little round fruit in early summer, kind of yellow to red, more like a small plum than anything else.
slots.description: Fruit shape/color — a round plum-type drupe distinguishes Chickasaw plum from the small hard greenish-brown pear fruit Callery pear produces.

slots.name: thorn_check
slots.value: There are some thorny little spurs on the branches here and there, but nothing huge or nasty.
slots.description: Thorn severity — Chickasaw plum may have thorny spurs, but nothing close to Callery pear's thorns up to a few inches long, capable of puncturing tires.

slots.name: growth_form
slots.value: It's more of a bushy, multi-stemmed thing than one single trunk going straight up.
slots.description: Growth habit — Chickasaw plum is a shrub-like, thicket-forming plant, distinct from Callery pear's upright, single-trunk tree form.

slots.name: bloom_appearance
slots.value: It had a bunch of small white flowers on it back in early spring.
slots.description: Distractor: both Chickasaw plum and Callery pear bloom white flowers in early-to-mid spring, so bloom timing/appearance alone does not distinguish them — the fruit and growth-form slots are what actually matter.

slots.name: planting_location
slots.value: It's growing near the back corner of the yard by some other bushes.
slots.description: Distractor: location in the yard has no bearing on identification here.

slots.name: how_long_present
slots.value: It's been there since we moved in a few years ago — didn't plant it ourselves.
slots.description: Distractor: how long the tree has been on the property doesn't change the correct identification or framing.

ecological_framing_notes: Chickasaw plum is a native thicket-forming tree that NC State Extension recommends planting as a replacement when an actual Callery pear is removed — it provides cover for songbirds and small mammals and supports pollinators and butterfly larvae. A correct answer should identify it as Chickasaw plum (not Callery pear), citing the round plum-type fruit and shrubbier growth form rather than bloom timing alone (both species bloom similarly in spring), note that no removal is needed, and ideally encourage keeping it.
